summary: The same IP prefix may be advertised by several routers as anycast, and other routers benefit from knowing that. This Standards Track document defines a new flag in the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags to advertise the anycast property, plus a companion YANG module.

plainLanguage.summary: Many shops share the same address. A sign tells travelers that more than one shop has it, so they can pick the nearest.

questions: how does ospf advertise anycast prefixes
what happens if n-flag and ac-flag are both set
subtitle: A new OSPFv2 flag tells routers that a prefix is anycast, advertised by more than one node.

tldr.problem: An IP prefix may be configured as anycast, so several routers advertise the same value, and it is useful for other routers to know that. OSPFv2 had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9983 defines the AC-Flag, value 0x10, in the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags. It also provides a companion YANG module to configure it.
tldr.outcome: Routers can tell anycast prefixes from node-specific ones, and BGP-LS carries the same flag. Receivers must allow for misconfiguration when relying on it.

today: RFC 9983 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
An IP prefix may be configured as anycast, so the same value can be advertised by multiple routers. RFC 7684 defines OSPFv2 Opaque LSAs built from Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples. The OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV, carried in the Extended Prefix Opaque LSA, advertises extra attributes of a prefix.

Anycast extensions already exist for IS-IS (RFC 9352) and OSPFv3 (RFC 9513). This document adds one for OSPFv2, as a flag in the Flags field of the Extended Prefix TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers share maps of where addresses live. This document adds a small label to the OSPFv2 map that says an address is shared by several places.

sections.title: The AC-Flag
sections.content:
The RFC adds a flag to the "OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags" registry: value 0x10, the Anycast Flag (AC-Flag). Its only meaning is that the prefix is intended to be advertised by multiple nodes. When a prefix is configured as anycast the flag MUST be set; otherwise it MUST be clear.

If at least one router sets the flag for a prefix, the prefix is considered anycast. A prefix advertised by a single node without the flag is considered node-specific. The flag MUST be preserved when the Extended Prefix Opaque LSA is re-advertised into other areas.

Anycast prefixes SHOULD be consistently managed throughout the network. Because a set flag takes precedence, stale configurations should be strictly monitored.
sections.plainLanguage: If any one shop puts up the 'shared address' sign, everybody treats the address as shared. The sign must also stay on when the news is passed to other neighborhoods.

sections.title: Conflict with the N-flag
sections.content: The AC-Flag and the N-flag (Section 2.1 of RFC 7684) MUST NOT both be set. A received advertisement with both set is a configuration anomaly: the N-flag MUST be ignored, and the conflict SHOULD be logged as an operational error, subject to rate-limiting.
sections.plainLanguage: A sign cannot say 'only one shop has this address' and 'many shops have this address' at once. If it does, the 'many shops' sign wins and someone is told about the mistake.

sections.title: BGP-LS Advertisement
sections.content: RFC 9085 defines the Prefix Attribute Flags TLV for BGP-LS. Its Flags field is interpreted according to OSPFv2 (RFC 7684), so it also conveys the anycast property introduced here with no further definition needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The same sign is automatically understood by another system that copies routers' maps, so nothing extra has to be invented.

sections.title: The YANG Module
sections.content:
The companion module ietf-ospf-anycast-flag is a YANG data model, usable through NETCONF or RESTCONF. It augments the OSPF YANG model (RFC 9129) and the routing management model (RFC 8349).

It adds a boolean anycast-flag leaf to each OSPFv2 interface, defaulting to false. A must constraint stops it from being true while the node flag is also true. The module also defines an identity ac-flag for the new Extended Prefix flag.
sections.plainLanguage: There is also a switch in the router's settings. Flip it on, and the router puts the 'shared address' sign on that address.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content: IANA allocated 0x10 (AC-Flag) in the "OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags" registry. It also registered the XML namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ospf-anycast-flag and the YANG module name ietf-ospf-anycast-flag with prefix ospf-anycast-flag.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of flag numbers now has the new sign written in it, along with the name of the settings module.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol extension does not affect the OSPFv2 security model. However, correct interpretation of the flag depends on router support and accurate operator configuration, so receivers MUST consider possible misconfiguration or inconsistent implementation when relying on it for forwarding or security decisions.

For the YANG module, the anycast-flag node is writable and readable. Unprotected writes could prevent a prefix from being interpreted as anycast or node-specific, and unauthorized reads could disclose anycast property information. Management protocols must use secure transport and mutual authentication, and NACM can restrict access.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks in and flips the switch wrongly, routers could be misled. So the settings must be protected, and routers should not blindly trust the sign.

items.title: Anycast
items.text: At least one advertiser sets the AC-Flag (0x10).

items.title: Node-specific
items.text: Advertised by a single node without the AC-Flag.

items.title: Anomaly
items.text: Both AC-Flag and N-flag set: N-flag is ignored and the conflict is logged.
